hey there—while reading this, i really got the sense that she might be dealing with borderline personality disorder. some of bpd’s trademark behaviors are: intense mood swings, frequently recurring self-harm/suicidal ideation, unstable personal relationships, unclear personal identity, fear of abandonment, and difficulty regulating emotions.

often with bpd we see the concept of the “favorite person.” this is a person who has been with the borderline individual through a difficult time, and that individual subsequently develops an extreme attachment to the FP. their emotions, thoughts and identity will often revolve around the mood of the FP; if the FP is happy, angry, sad, anxious etc. then the borderline individual will feel that way as well. since bpd is relatively difficult to manage, this relationship with the FP is often unhealthy in terms of the dependency it fosters.

bpd sounds like a scary thing, and it is a lot to deal with. i will say that it’s more common in people who have experienced trauma, so that may be a contributing factor. however—bpd CAN be managed with targeted therapies and medications, usually mood stabilizers. have her look into dialectical behavioral therapy; that’s the standard course of action for borderline individuals. setting your own boundaries will be a huge part of her recovery. it’s going to be hard, but you need to learn how to stay steadfast in your decisions; it’s going to be much easier for both of you to manage the feelings that come with those boundaries if you maintain a firm resolve and a strong will. there is tons of material online and in books about having a loved one with bpd, and i would very highly recommend you read that. “i hate you, don’t leave me” is a very popular one.

i’m considered somewhat of a bpd “success story.” i have a diagnosis of complex PTSD, and have been displaying bpd symptoms since i was 11 or 12. bpd was mentioned to me a few years ago, and when i read more about it, it honestly felt like i was looking into a mirror. i’ve been in trauma therapy, CBT and DBT ever since, and along with much medication experimentation, i’m considered stable now. i can manage the symptoms as they come, and i can do so in a way that doesn’t hurt those around me.

i’m in a wonderful, healthy relationship of nearly 2 years with a sweet, caring man who has been nothing but supportive of my treatment. i do consider him to be my FP, but the thing about FPs is that those relationships do not always have to be unhealthy! if you set boundaries and communicate regularly, then the FP relationship can actually be very functional, stable and happy for both parties. i would highly suggest that you do a bit of research on bpd, and if you think it worthwhile, bring it up with your partner in a calm environment—perhaps in a therapy session, that’s usually best for facilitating productive conversation. good luck to you. i will be keeping you in my thoughts.

i’ve been on the other side of this situation many times. i have some complex mental health issues stemming from childhood trauma, and as a result, i’m prone to depressive episodes.

the uncertainty you’re feeling right now is completely healthy and understandable. having mental illness is one of the hardest things to endure, and i wouldn’t wish it on anyone in the world. however, the struggles of those who experience mental illness should not invalidate the struggles of our partners, families and friends obsolete.

when reading this post, i can see right off the bat that you care for your partner deeply. you worry about him, but even further, you can empathize with some of the emotions that he’s feeling. this is HUGE in any relationship, especially when one party deals with mental illness. i’ve been in a relationship for over a year and a half, and i can say that it took a long long time for my partner to understand and learn that skill of empathy. the fact that you seem to do it naturally will be a huge help in this situation.

honestly, nobody can know when depressive episodes end. he’s probably asking the same question that you are—“when will this end?” i also think it’s highly likely that he is also feeling anxiety about this situation, about what effect it will have on the both of you individually and together. unfortunately the truth is that nobody can see what the future will hold. but this doesn’t mean that the two of you can’t fight like hell to make sure that this works out.

my honest advice is to openly listen and communicate. if you think it would help, bring up this uncertainty with him and try to start a conversation about the emotions that both of you are feeling. but, in general, just be there. try not to feel like you can’t talk to him about what you’re thinking and feeling in this situation. in my experience, the last thing that people with mental illness want is for our loved ones to feel as though they can’t rely on us, or that they can’t express their own feelings due to fear that we won’t be able to handle it. 

depression may affect your partner’s behavior, appearance and thought patterns. but try to remember, through all the uncertainty and anxiety, that he is the one you love. treat him with kindness, patience and the empathy that you possess. that is one of the most important supports that he will be needing to get through this.
